questions.question: How does the extension host communicate with the main process?

facts.fact: Both sides talk through the same RPCProtocol class: getProxy(identifier) returns a JS Proxy that turns any $-prefixed method call into _remoteCall, which serializes a request (rpcId, method name, args), sends it on the message-passing protocol and returns a promise, while the receiving side's _receiveOneMessage/_receiveRequest/_doInvokeHandler calls that method on the object registered with set(identifier, instance), sends an Acknowledged message, then a ReplyOK or ReplyErr message that settles the caller's promise.

The contract is declared in extHost.protocol.ts: MainThread*Shape interfaces with MainContext identifiers (implemented on the main/workbench side and called from the extension host) and ExtHost*Shape interfaces with ExtHostContext identifiers (implemented in the extension host and called from the workbench), each identifier created with createProxyIdentifier, which assigns a numeric id (nid) used on the wire.

The 'main' end of this RPC for the desktop local extension host is the workbench in the renderer (window) process, not the Electron main process: ExtensionHostManager._createExtensionHostCustomers creates the RPCProtocol there, instantiates every MainThread* class registered with @extHostNamedCustomer (ExtHostCustomersRegistry), sets each as the local actor for its MainContext id, and asserts that all MainContext ids are registered.

On desktop the local extension host is an Electron utility process: the renderer asks the main-process ExtensionHostStarter (over the 'extensionHostStarter' IPC channel) to create and start it, WindowUtilityProcess.start forks vs/workbench/api/node/extensionHostProcess with utilityProcess.fork, creates a MessageChannelMain, gives one port to the utility process and posts the other to the window on 'vscode:startExtensionHostMessagePortResult' with a nonce, and from then on the renderer and the extension host exchange messages directly over that MessagePort instead of relaying through the main process.

Before RPC starts there is a raw handshake: the extension host sends a Ready message, the renderer replies with the JSON-serialized IExtensionHostInitData, the extension host answers Initialized (MessageType Ready/Initialized/Terminate in extensionHostProtocol.ts), and Terminate is later used to ask the extension host to shut down gracefully.

Each RPC message is a binary buffer that starts with a 1-byte MessageType and a 4-byte request id; the types are RequestJSONArgs/RequestMixedArgs (each with a WithCancellation variant), Acknowledged, Cancel, ReplyOKEmpty/ReplyOKVSBuffer/ReplyOKJSON/ReplyOKJSONWithBuffers and ReplyErrError/ReplyErrEmpty, with arguments JSON-stringified except VSBuffer and SerializableObjectWithBuffers values, which are sent as binary.

Inside the extension host, ExtensionHostMain wraps the connected protocol in its own RPCProtocol (with a URI transformer for remote), exposes it as IExtHostRpcService, and createApiFactoryAndRegisterActors registers the ExtHost* actors with rpcProtocol.set and asserts every ExtHostContext id is registered, while API implementations call the workbench via rpcProtocol.getProxy(MainContext.X).

Other extension host kinds reuse the same RPCProtocol over different transports: the remote extension host over a PersistentProtocol socket from connectRemoteAgentExtensionHost, the web worker extension host over a MessagePort to a hidden iframe/worker, and extensionHostProcess.ts also supports IPC-pipe and Socket connections (ExtHostConnectionType) wrapped in PersistentProtocol.

questions.question: This question follows on from "How does the extension host communicate with the main process?"; "that path" means the communication path between the extension host and the main process. Where in that path would a message be dropped if the extension host crashes?

facts.fact: The renderer learns of the crash only through the exit event of the utility process: ExtensionHostStarter.onDynamicExit (WindowUtilityProcess.onExit, fired from the process 'exit' event) reaches NativeLocalProcessExtensionHost._onExtHostProcessExit, which fires onExit unless the host was being terminated on purpose (_terminating), and the main process also logs the exit and force-kills the pid if it still exists 1 s later.

That exit is handled by AbstractExtensionService._onExtensionHostCrashOrExit -> _onExtensionHostCrashed, which for a LocalProcess host calls _doStopExtensionHosts, whose ExtensionHostCollection.stopAllInReverse disconnects and disposes every extension host manager, and ExtensionHostManager.dispose disposes its RPCProtocol.

RPCProtocol.dispose sets _isDisposed and rejects every entry in _pendingRPCReplies with a canceled error, so requests already sent to the crashed extension host never get a reply and their callers see a cancellation instead.

After disposal, _remoteCall returns a CanceledLazyPromise without sending anything, so new proxy calls are dropped, and _receiveOneMessage returns immediately, so any late incoming message is ignored (replies for unknown request ids are also ignored by _receiveReply/_receiveReplyErr).

Between the crash and the exit notification nothing checks delivery: the renderer's send is a fire-and-forget port.postMessage on the MessagePort, and the only signal is that unacknowledged requests make RPCProtocol switch to ResponsiveState.Unresponsive after 3 s (UNRESPONSIVE_TIME), which ExtensionHostManager forwards and AbstractExtensionService logs as 'unresponsive'.

During that shutdown NativeLocalProcessExtensionHost.disconnect tries to send a Terminate message (waiting at most 1 s for the protocol) and swallows any error, so with a crashed host the Terminate message is silently lost.

Lost messages are not replayed: NativeExtensionService._onExtensionHostCrashed restarts the extension hosts automatically unless this is the third crash within 5 minutes (ExtensionHostCrashTracker), and the restarted host gets a fresh RPCProtocol and only re-runs previously requested activation events (_allRequestedActivateEvents).

By contrast, socket-based connections (remote extension host) use PersistentProtocol, which keeps unacknowledged messages in _outgoingUnackMsg and resends them after reconnection, so a temporary connection loss does not drop messages; the extension host process terminates itself only if the renderer does not reconnect within the reconnection grace time.

questions.question: This question follows on from "How does the extension host communicate with the main process?"; "that protocol" means the protocol the extension host uses to talk to the main process, and "a new message type" means a new kind of call that the extension host can make to the main side. What would I need to change to add a new message type to that protocol?

facts.fact: Declare the call in extHost.protocol.ts: add a $-prefixed method to an existing MainThread*Shape interface, or define a new MainThreadXShape and add an entry MainThreadX: createProxyIdentifier<MainThreadXShape>('MainThreadX') to MainContext.

The method name must start with $ because RPCProtocol's proxy only synthesizes remote stubs for property names whose first character is '$' (CharCode.DollarSign), forwarding them to _remoteCall(rpcId, name, args).

Implement it on the main side in a MainThreadX class under src/vs/workbench/api/browser/ decorated with @extHostNamedCustomer(MainContext.MainThreadX), and import that file from extensionHost.contribution.ts so the decorator runs and ExtensionHostManager instantiates it and registers it with rpcProtocol.set for every extension host.

A new MainContext identifier without a registered customer breaks extension host startup: MainThreadExtensionService passes all MainContext identifiers through _setAllMainProxyIdentifiers, and _createExtensionHostCustomers calls assertRegistered, which throws 'Missing proxy instance <id>'.

Call it from the extension host via rpcProtocol.getProxy(MainContext.MainThreadX).$method(...) (IExtHostRpcService), usually inside an ExtHostX class; if the main side must call back, also add an ExtHostXShape with an ExtHostContext entry and register the instance with rpcProtocol.set(ExtHostContext.ExtHostX, ...) in createApiFactoryAndRegisterActors, where assertRegistered(Object.values(ExtHostContext)) checks it.

Arguments and results must survive serialization, as the Proxied<T>/Dto<T> types express: values are JSON-stringified (functions are dropped), VSBuffer and SerializableObjectWithBuffers go as binary, URIs travel as UriComponents to be revived (and transformed for remote), and a trailing CancellationToken argument becomes a WithCancellation request plus a Cancel message.

No change is needed in the wire layer, because requests carry the rpcId (one byte, writeUInt8) and the method name generically; only a new wire-level kind would need a new MessageType enum value, new MessageIO serialize/deserialize methods and a new case in RPCProtocol._receiveOneMessage, whose default branch logs 'received unexpected message'.

To expose the feature to extensions, the API also has to be added to src/vscode-dts/vscode.d.ts (or a vscode.proposed.*.d.ts proposal) and wired into the vscode namespace object that createApiFactoryAndRegisterActors returns.

questions.question: How does the keybinding service resolve a chord to a command?

facts.fact: WorkbenchKeybindingService registers keydown and keyup listeners on every window (_registerKeyListeners); keydown wraps the event in a StandardKeyboardEvent and calls _dispatch, and keyup feeds _singleModifierDispatch for single-modifier chords such as 'shift shift'.

The keyboard event is converted to a ResolvedKeybinding by the layout-aware keyboard mapper (resolveKeyboardEvent -> _keyboardMapper.resolveKeyboardEvent, using MacLinux/Windows/Fallback keyboard mappers), and getDispatchChords() gives the dispatch string for the pressed chord.

AbstractKeybindingService._doDispatch takes the context for the event target from the context key service (getContext(target)) and calls KeybindingResolver.resolve(context, currentChords, keypress), where currentChords are the chords already pressed in an ongoing multi-chord sequence (_currentChords).

KeybindingResolver.resolve looks up the candidates for the first chord in _map, keeps those whose later chords match the chords pressed so far, and _findCommand scans them from the end (later, higher-priority entries win) for the first whose when clause evaluates true; it returns MoreChordsNeeded if that keybinding has more chords than were pressed, KbFound(command, args, bubble) otherwise, and NoMatchingKb when nothing matches.

On MoreChordsNeeded the service stores the chord in _currentChords, shows the status message '(...) was pressed. Waiting for second key of chord...' and leaves chord mode after 5 s or when the window loses focus; on KbFound it leaves chord mode and runs ICommandService.executeCommand(commandId, args); on NoMatchingKb during chord mode it shows 'The key combination (...) is not a command.' and leaves chord mode.

The resolver is built lazily in WorkbenchKeybindingService._getResolver from KeybindingsRegistry.getDefaultKeybindings() (core rules plus extension-contributed keybindings, sorted by weight from EditorCore to ExternalExtension) followed by the user's keybindings.json entries, after handleRemovals applies '-command' removals, and it is rebuilt when keybindings, extensions or the keyboard layout change.
CommandService.executeCommand fires the onCommand:<id> activation event (activating the contributing extension if needed) and then runs the handler registered in CommandsRegistry.
Keystrokes that are part of an IME composition are not dispatched (_dispatch returns false when isKeyInComposition(e)).
